phonemes.desc: Rough breathing plus upsilon: a breathy /h/ before the close front rounded vowel /y/ — a sound English lacks, nearest to French 'tu' or German 'über'.
Unaspirated /p/ followed by a short, open /e/; light and quick, carrying no stress.
A trilled /r/ closing on short iota, which bears the acute accent — the high pitch of the word falls here.
Long omega (ω), held roughly twice the length of a short vowel, closed by the final nasal; the length is part of the name, not an ornament.

pronunciation.approximation: 'hü-peh-REE-ohn' — round the lips for Hy- (the ü of German 'über'), strike the accent hard on -rí-, and let the final -ōn ring long.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ὑπέρ (hyper), 'over, above, beyond' — the name parses as 'he who goes above', the Titan of the upper sky

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *upér, 'over' — whence Latin super, Sanskrit upári, and English both 'over' and the prefix 'hyper-'

pronunciation.note: Tier-1: the Greek original Ὑπερίων carries both a stress mark (the acute on the iota) and a long vowel (ω), and the restoration Hyperíōn preserves both — the í keeps the accent where Hesiod's auditors heard it, and the ō keeps the quantity of the omega. Both features survive in the Unicode form; the ASCII 'Hyperion' loses them.

domains.title: The Father of Lights
domains.subtitle: Light, Heavenly Watch
domains.lead: Hyperíōn is the High One — the Titan whose very name, from ὑπέρ, means 'he who goes above'. Hesiod makes him the bridge between the raw sky and its fires: son of Ouranos and Gaia, husband of Theía, and father of every light that crosses the heavens — Hēlios the Sun, Selḗnē the Moon, and Ēṓs the Dawn (Theogony 371–374). He has almost no story of his own; he is the genealogy of light itself, and in Homer his name is already spoken as a name of the sun.

cards.name: Celestial Light
cards.desc: Hesiod names him father of the three lights that cross the sky — Hēlios the Sun, Selḗnē the Moon, Ēṓs the Dawn (Theogony 371–374).

cards.name: The Heavenly Watch
cards.desc: His name runs from ὑπέρ, 'he who goes above', and Homer already speaks Hyperíōn as a name of the sun itself (Iliad 8.480).

cards.name: Progenitor of the Luminaries
cards.desc: With Theía he begets every luminary; later poets fold his name into his son’s until Titan and Sun are spoken as one.

symbols.name: The Vault of Heaven
symbols.meaning: His name declares it: from ὑπέρ, 'above', he is 'he who goes above' — the upper sky made personal, the height from which all light descends.

symbols.name: The Sun's Rays
symbols.meaning: In Iliad 8 (479–481) the rays are 'of Hyperion the Sun' (Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο) — Homer speaks the name as a solar title, whether patronymic or epithet.

symbols.name: The Chariot of Day
symbols.meaning: Through his son Hēlios, who drives the four-horse chariot across the sky each day; later poets collapse father and son, and 'Hyperion' rides as the sun itself.

symbols.name: The Three Luminaries
symbols.meaning: Sun, Moon, and Dawn — his children by Theía (Theogony 371–374); his true emblem is genealogical, the whole family of sky-lights.

symbols.name: The Watchman's Station
symbols.meaning: As the one above, he holds the high lookout of heaven — the Titan whose vantage is the zenith itself, from which nothing on earth is hidden.

symbols.name: The Chains of Tartarus
symbols.meaning: After the Titanomachy he shares the Titans' prison 'as far beneath the earth as heaven is above the earth' (Theogony 717–720) — the High One brought low.

mythology.lead: Hyperíōn is a Titan of lineage rather than adventure: Hesiod gives him a birth, a marriage, three luminous children, and a fall — and almost nothing else. His myths are the myths of what his name means and of what his name became.

myths.title: A Son of Heaven and Earth
myths.text: In Theogony (132–136), Hesiod catalogues the children Gaia bore to Ouranos: the deep-swirling Ocean, then Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, and Iapetus, and with them the Titanesses — Theía, Rheía, Thémis, Mnēmosýnē, Phoíbē, and Tēthýs — and finally Krónos, 'crooked-counselled, the most terrible of her children'. Hyperíōn enters the poem with no deed attached, only a station: his name already declares it, from ὑπέρ, 'above'. He is born of the union of Sky and Earth and belongs to the sky's own house. Hesiod's silence about his character is itself telling — this Titan is a fixture of the high order of things, not a personality.

myths.title: Father of Sun, Moon, and Dawn
myths.text: In Theogony (371–374), Hyperíōn takes his sister Theía — 'the divine one' — to wife, and she bears him Hēlios the Sun, Selḗnē the Moon, and Ēṓs the Dawn, 'who shines on all that dwell on the earth and on the deathless gods who hold broad heaven'. The marriage is a small cosmology in itself: the High One wed to the Divine produces every light that crosses the sky. Pindar opens Isthmian 5 by addressing Theía as 'mother of the Sun, of many names', the hymn-like acknowledgement of this same union. Through his children, Hyperíōn is present at every sunrise, moonrise, and daybreak — he never leaves the sky he fathered onto it.

myths.title: Hyperion in Homer
myths.text: Homer never treats Hyperíōn as a separate god: the name arrives already fused with the sun. In Iliad 8 (479–481), Zeus pictures the nether gloom where Iápetos and Krónos sit 'rejoicing neither in the rays of Hyperion the Sun (Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο) nor in the winds', and Odyssey 1 (8) opens the Thrinakía story with the same compound, 'Hyperion the Sun'. Scholars divide honestly on the grammar: is Ὑπερίων here a patronymic — the Sun as 'son of Hyperion' — or an epithet — the Sun himself as 'the one above'? Both readings have ancient defenders, and later Greek and Roman poets simply settle it by usage, letting 'Hyperion' stand alone as the sun. The ambiguity is old and probably unresolvable; it is also the whole point — the Titan's name was always tending toward the light.

myths.title: Cast into Tartarus
myths.text: In Theogony (717–720), after ten years of war between the Titans and the Olympians, Zeus and his allies bind the defeated Titans and hurl them into Tartarus, 'as far beneath the earth as heaven is above the earth; for so far is it from earth to murky Tartarus'. Hyperíōn, who stood with the Titans against Zeus, shares that fall; Hesiod names the prisoners collectively and gives him no individual scene. The poetic logic is stark: the one called 'he who goes above' is sent to the deepest below, where the rays that Homer calls his cannot reach. His children ride free overhead — the lights of the sky survive their father's imprisonment.

lore.syncretism: Rome produced no native Hyperion; the Titan travelled into Latin letters chiefly as a learned name for the sun itself, the Hesiodic father and the Homeric epithet collapsing into one solar word in the poets. Hyginus still lists him soberly among the Titans born of Earth and Sky (Fabulae, praefatio), but in later epic usage 'Hyperion' rides the sky in place of Sol. What survived of him in the West was thus not a cult but a word — the most elevated name Latin poetry knew for the sun.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hyperíōn's deepest modern life is linguistic: the English prefix 'hyper-' (hyperactive, hyperlink, hyperspace) descends from ὑπέρ, the very root of his name — every 'hyper-' word unknowingly repeats 'he who goes above'. The Titan himself was given fresh stature by Keats's unfinished epic Hyperion (1820), which made his fall after the Titanomachy a meditation on the succession of gods. Astronomers named Saturn's moon Hyperion at its discovery in 1848, and the tallest known living tree on Earth, a coast redwood in California, was named Hyperion in 2006 — the High One still lends his name to things that out-top everything around them.
lore.extendedMeditation: The Greeks gave Hyperíōn almost no cult, no temple, and no character — and that absence is the datum a scholar should trust. He is less a god one worshipped than a piece of the world's grammar: the name that lets Hesiod explain why the sky has lights, and lets Homer call the sun by its noblest title. There is a quiet ambivalence in him: a defeated Titan, chained in the dark below Tartarus' gates, whose name nevertheless means the summit and whose children are the daily proofs of heaven's order. In Hyperíōn the Greeks caught a truth about succession — the old order falls, but what it fathered goes on shining. He endures as the rare Titan whose legacy is not a deed but a direction: upward.
lore.archaeology: No temple, sanctuary, or civic cult of Hyperíōn is securely attested anywhere in the Greek world; Pausanias, who records altars of such Titans as Kronos and Iapetus, offers him no shrine. He was honoured, if at all, within the cult of his son Hēlios — above all at Rhodes, where the Sun received a major state cult and the great bronze Colossus — so his archaeological trace survives only folded into his children's worship. His monument is textual rather than stone: the name that Homer and Hesiod carved into the language of light.
